extracted.intended_audience: wealthy individuals, philanthropists, civic leaders, and policymakers thinking about charitable giving
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for wealthy persons about how to dispose of surplus wealth and conduct philanthropy during their lives so as to best benefit the community; identifies what to fund, how to give, and what practices to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper administration of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth should be administered to preserve social cohesion between rich and poor; the essay frames philanthropy as a social duty to maintain harmonious relations and the progress of civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of competition, accumulation, and inequality as foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay assumes “the present laws of competition, accumulation, and distribution are the best obtainable conditions” and that great inequality is inevitable under them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie argues donors should work within these economic realities rather than attempt radical systemic overthrow; this informs what kinds of philanthropic interventions are practical and desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of disposing surplus wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are but three modes in which surplus wealth can be disposed of. It can be left to the families of the decedents; or it can be bequeathed for public purposes; or, finally, it can be administered during their lives by its possessors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie analyzes each mode and endorses lifetime administration as the best; the rubric treats these three options as mutually exclusive choices with distinct consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leaving great fortunes to children
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving great fortunes to children is usually injudicious: “If this is done from affection, is it not misguided affection?... it is not the welfare of the children, but family pride, which inspires these enormous legacies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bequests to heirs often harm recipients and the state; moderate provision for dependents is acceptable, but not enormous legacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about bequests at death for public uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Bequests left at death are often ineffective: they may become “monuments of his folly,” be thwarted, or need the same ability to execute as was required to amass wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posthumous gifts can fail through legal contest, misadministration, or unintended effects; prefer active lifetime administration where possible (examples: Tilden, Williamson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surplus wealth during life as a sacred trust
rubrics_metrics.description: “Surplus wealth should be considered as a sacred trust, to be administered during the lives of its owners, by them as trustees, for the best good of the community in which and from which it had been acquired.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donors are to act as trustees and agents, applying their wisdom and administrative ability to realize the greatest long-term public benefit rather than hoarding or late bequests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set an example of modest, unostentatious living
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of wealth should “set an example of modest, unostentatious living, shunning display or extravagance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public modesty is part of the duty of wealth; ostentation offends public sentiment and undermines the moral example of the donor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide only moderate maintenance for dependents
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide “moderately for the legitimate wants of those dependent upon him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support for family should be reasonable and not translate into vast fortunes that harm the recipients or the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat surplus revenues as trust funds to be administered for community good
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider “all surplus revenues which come to him simply as trust funds, which he is called upon to administer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surplus is not personal largesse but a fiduciary resource to be managed with the aim of producing the most beneficial results for the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indiscriminate charity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of every thousand dollars spent in so-called charity, it is probable that $950 is unwisely spent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indiscriminate giving often harms recipients (pauperizing, encouraging vice); donors should be deliberate and selective rather than giving impulsively to individual beggars or solicitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aid those who will help themselves (promote self-improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main consideration should be “to help those who will help themselves; to provide part of the means by which those who desire to improve may do so.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor programs and institutions that create ladders of advancement (education, training, public resources) rather than one-off alms that foster dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit direct individual giving because of lack of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual donor’s lack of detailed knowledge makes widespread individual giving unwise: “The amount which can be wisely given by the individual for individuals is necessarily limited by his lack of knowledge of the circumstances connected with each.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer institutional giving where the donor's funds are multiplied and better directed by knowledgeable administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer funding ‘ladders’ (free libraries, parks, recreation, art, public institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best means include placing “within [the public’s] reach the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise–free libraries, parks, and means of recreation, ... works of art, certain to give pleasure and improve the public taste, and public institutions of various kinds.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These investments are argued to yield intergenerational benefit, fostering aspiration and cultural improvement rather than temporary relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found or endow universities and observatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Founding a university or supporting scientific institutions (e.g., Lick Observatory) is singled out as a noble and lasting use of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale educational and scientific endowments require significant sums and attention but provide durable public goods and are highly meritorious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support hospitals, medical colleges, and research laboratories (emphasize prevention and training)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The founding or extension of hospitals, medical colleges, laboratories, and other institutions connected with the alleviation of human suffering, and especially with the prevention rather than the cure of human ills.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical research, training (e.g., nursing schools), and preventive measures are prime philanthropic targets because they relieve suffering without pauperizing communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide parks, conservatories, and urban beautification (with municipal maintenance requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public parks and associated features (conservatories, fountains, memorial arches) are recommended; donors should often require the city to maintain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditioning gifts on public maintenance secures permanence, public ownership, and ongoing civic interest (example: Mr. Phipps’s conservatories open on Sundays, with city maintenance stipulated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support museums, art galleries, and aesthetic improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting and displaying pictures, founding museums and galleries, and funding artistic ornamentation are proper uses of surplus wealth to reach and elevate the best of the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic works reach those with latent sensibilities and improve public taste; such gifts are valuable even if their material benefit is less immediately visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide public halls and venues for lectures and concerts
rubrics_metrics.description: Give towns halls or concert halls “suitable for meetings of all kinds, especially for concerts of elevating music.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public performance and meeting spaces, ideally municipally owned or maintained and rented cheaply, enrich civic life and broaden access to culture and education (Springer Hall example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide public swimming baths with nominal charge and municipal upkeep
rubrics_metrics.description: Give swimming baths, requiring the city to maintain them and usually charging a nominal fee while admitting schoolchildren free at fixed hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baths promote public health, teach swimming (life-saving), and should be structured to encourage upkeep and responsible use rather than free unlimited charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church gifts acceptable but are sectarian; donor should give the building only
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts to churches are sectarian and not strictly gifts to the whole community; it is appropriate to replace poor structures with permanent ones, but donors should stop at the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donors may fund the creation of worthy religious architecture but should not assume ongoing support of church operations; maintenance/support should be local.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition gifts on community maintenance and public ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Donors should often stipulate that the municipality maintain the gift so that it becomes public property and subject to public oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions ensure the gift’s permanence and alignment with public interest; examples include conservatories and parks where city maintenance was required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donor’s personal involvement and managerial attention are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The best gifts often require the time and attention of the giver: “They deserve credit ... as much for the time and the attention given during their lives, as for their expenditure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philanthropic success often depends on the donor contributing business sense, oversight, and dedication, not merely money (examples: Stanford, Springer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating dependence or rewarding vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts that “encourage the slothful, the drunken, the unworthy” are injurious; almsgiving more often rewards vice than relieves virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donors should aim to avoid funding programs or practices that promote idleness or dependency; instead, favor structures that require effort, merit, or participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philanthropy should stimulate aspiration rather than satisfy immediate appetites
rubrics_metrics.description: The rich should seek to give “the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise,” not small sums that may be wasted on appetite or indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize investments that promote long-term improvement (education, institutions) rather than temporary consumption or one-off handouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match philanthropic choice to donor’s conviction and enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrator should be “enthusiastically devoted to it and feel that in the field selected his work lies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness is enhanced when donors work in fields that align with their judgment and passion; diverse forms of benefaction are valid when well-chosen and sincerely supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public sentiment as a standard of modesty and propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Though exact amounts are undefinable, “Public sentiment is quick to know and to feel what offends these” (good taste/modesty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donors should be aware that community norms will judge extravagance or ostentation; using public sentiment as a guide helps determine what counts as modest and appropriate giving.
